report:
## Conclusion: Your skepticism is well-supported

The best available evidence backs your view — ginkgo biloba does **not** reliably relieve tinnitus symptoms.

The most authoritative source is the **Cochrane systematic review**, considered the gold standard for evaluating medical evidence. It concluded that the limited, mostly low-quality evidence "does not demonstrate that Ginkgo biloba is effective for tinnitus" and that the herb "may have little to no effect" on tinnitus severity compared with placebo (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6926930/). This finding is echoed in a summary of the same review noting it "concluded that the limited evidence does not demonstrate that Ginkgo biloba is effective for tinnitus" (https://scienceinsights.org/does-ginkgo-biloba-help-with-tinnitus-the-real-evidence/).

A separate meta-analysis by Rejali et al. specifically pooled randomized trials using various ginkgo products and concluded flatly that "Ginkgo biloba does not benefit patients with tinnitus" — a finding cited even within a more favorable review of a specific proprietary extract (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3157487/). Additional independent analysis using the standard Tinnitus Handicap Inventory found no significant difference between ginkgo and placebo groups (Mean Difference = -1.5, 95% CI: -4.0 to 1.0) (https://americanmedicalpublication.org/tajnm/article/view/215).

**Important nuance:** Some industry-funded or manufacturer-linked reviews of one specific standardized extract (EGb 761®) report modest positive effects, and results across studies are inconsistent partly due to varying ginkgo formulations and study quality. However, when independent, high-quality randomized controlled trials are pooled together, the consensus is that ginkgo shows no convincing benefit over placebo for tinnitus loudness, distress, or quality of life. Your conclusion — "no" — aligns with the strongest evidence available.
